title: Benjamin Franklin and His Loyalist Son
text:
William Franklin was Benjamin Franklin's son, born out of wedlock around 1730 and raised in his father's household. The two were close. William helped with his father's electrical experiments, traveled with him to London, and with his father's influence became royal governor of New Jersey in 1763.

When the American Revolution came, they chose opposite sides. Benjamin became one of the leaders of independence. William stayed loyal to the king. In 1776 he was arrested by the patriots and imprisoned in Connecticut in harsh conditions. His wife, Elizabeth, died in 1777 in New York while he was held; he was not allowed to see her. His father did not intervene. After his release in an exchange, William led loyalist forces in New York and then left for England in 1782.

In 1784 Benjamin wrote to him that nothing had ever hurt him so much as finding himself deserted in old age by his only son, and not only deserted but opposed in arms, in a cause in which his good name, fortune and life were at stake.

In 1785 the two met briefly in Southampton, England. They spent the time settling business. In his will Franklin left William very little, explaining that the part he had played against his father in the war accounted for it. William's son, Temple, whom Benjamin had raised, sided with his grandfather.
lesson: Political division can break even the closest family ties. When loyalties collide, decide early whether the relationship matters more than winning the argument.
people: Benjamin Franklin, William Franklin, William Temple Franklin
location: Philadelphia and New Jersey, USA; Southampton, England (UK)
source: Benjamin Franklin to William Franklin, 16 August 1784; Franklin's will (1788); Sheila L. Skemp, William Franklin (1990)
